title: Does Expert Supervision Improve Text-to-Speech?An Empirical Study of Preference Optimization

paper.title: Does Expert Supervision Improve Text-to-Speech? An Empirical Study of Preference Optimization
paper.abstract: Abstract Preference optimization promises to improve text-to-speech (TTS) systems by learning which speech outputs are better. External expert speech seems a natural source of preferred responses, especially when student generations contain errors. Yet demonstration quality does not establish whether the student can benefit from that supervision, or whether better target fitting will produce better speech. We examine this gap across two TTS students using real and synthetic expert speech, comparing preference objectives and direct versus bridge supervision while tracking fixed-sequence likelihoods and generation metrics. With expert supervision held fixed, objectives differ markedly in their sensitivity to preference-score scaling and the resulting generation quality. Likelihood diagnostics characterize these responses, but cannot establish their benefit: expert likelihood can increase while intelligibility worsens, or decrease while it improves. Bridge supervision highlights a distinction between mitigating degradation and improving the student: it can recover performance lost under direct training without consistently surpassing the pretrained base. Route benefits vary across objectives, students, and expert sources; neither route consistently dominates. Together, these findings distinguish demonstration quality, target fitting, and generated-speech quality as complementary criteria for assessing expert supervision.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Preference optimization offers text-to-speech (TTS) systems a way to learn which speech outputs to prefer. Language-model-based TTS enables this approach through speech-token prediction ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2024 ; Casanova et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Anastassiou et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from chosen–rejected pairs without a separately trained reward model ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and has been applied to speech generation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Its appeal, however, depends on where those preferred responses come from. Figure 1: Motivating questions for expert-guided preference optimization. Schematic panels H1–H3 correspond to RQ1–RQ3: objective sensitivity, likelihood responses, and supervision routes. One option is to rank student generations using recognition or speaker metrics ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) . Another is to pair student generations with external demonstrations from real recordings or an expert synthesizer. We call the latter expert-guided preference optimization . Demonstrations supply preferred targets without ranking a pool of student candidates and can provide examples absent from that pool. The attraction is straightforward: teach the student to favor an expert’s response over its own. Whether this produces a better speech generator is less straightforward. Existing evidence cautions against equating demonstration quality with training benefit. TTS studies report limited gains from ground-truth chosen responses compared with ranked model outputs ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) , with related observations in non-verbal vocalization synthesis ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Expert speech must also pass through the student’s speech-token representation, which can alter its quality. During optimization, a larger preference margin can coexist with declining chosen-response likelihood ( Pal et al., 2024 ) ; such a decline need not imply worse generation ( Im et al., 2026 ) . These observations leave an empirical question: how does fitting expert targets relate to generation quality under different objectives and supervision routes? We study CosyVoice and GPT-SoVITS as students, with real recordings and Qwen3-TTS generations as expert sources. We compare DPO, Weighted Preference Optimization (WPO), Anchored Preference Optimization’s zero variant (APO-zero), and Noise Contrastive Alignment (NCA) ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . RQ1 examines sensitivity to the score scale β \beta , and RQ2 relates likelihood changes to generation outcomes. RQ3 asks how supervision routes affect these outcomes across objectives, expert sources, and students. We compare Direct training on full expert targets with a staged Bridge route. A Bridge target combines an expert prefix with a student-generated continuation, adapting a construction explored in InCo-DPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) to speech. This route introduces Bridge targets before full expert supervision and refreshes rejected responses between phases. The comparison evaluates the complete protocol. Fixed expert and initial-student probes make likelihood changes comparable across checkpoints even when training pairs change. Our study yields three findings about expert supervision: • Reconstruction can erode an expert’s intelligibility advantage, so source quality alone does not characterize the supervision received by the student. • Training benefits depend on the objective and supervision route: objectives differ in sensitivity to β \beta , while bridge supervision can mitigate degradation without consistently surpassing the pretrained base. • Expert-probe likelihood can increase while intelligibility worsens, or decrease while it improves; target fitting alone therefore cannot establish generation benefit.

sections.heading: 2.1 Post-Training for Speech Generation
sections.text: Speech post-training draws on reinforcement learning from human feedback ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and PPO/GRPO policy optimization ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . Seed-TTS, IndexTTS 2.5, and GLM-TTS optimize rewards for recognition accuracy, speaker consistency, or expressiveness ( Anastassiou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . Other work studies GRPO-based TTS and ASR-guided updates ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Hussain et al., 2026 ) , differentiable rewards ( Gao et al., 2025a ; Gao et al., 2025b ) , and metric optimization for diffusion synthesis and duration prediction ( Li et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . At inference, MSpoofTTS uses spoof detectors for pruning and reranking; TED-TTS controls emotion and duration without fine-tuning ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . DPO uses preference pairs; KTO uses individual desirability labels ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ) . Speech preferences often rank candidates by recognition or speaker metrics ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . UNO and RIO study unpaired feedback and reverse-inference supervision ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2024 ) ; FPO and TKTO study fine-grained and targeted token-level optimization ( Yao et al., 2026 ; Kotoge and Sasaki, 2026 ) . Align-SLM uses semantic feedback for speech continuation ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , while non-verbal synthesis requires preferences sensitive to lexical content and vocal events ( Li et al., 2026a ) . We compare how objectives use external expert demonstrations.

sections.heading: 2.2 Preference Data and Policy Compatibility
sections.text: Discrete latent learning ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ) and neural audio codecs ( Zeghidour et al., 2022 ; Défossez et al., 2022 ) support token-based audio modeling and reconstruction. AudioLM combines semantic and acoustic tokens for structure and acoustic detail ( Borsos et al., 2023 ) ; we evaluate expert speech before and after reconstruction through the student’s representation. SpeechAlign pairs encoded recordings with synthesized responses and refreshes the latter ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . However, ground-truth chosen responses yield limited benefits in some TTS studies ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) ; ground-truth and hybrid targets can also underperform synthetic pairs in non-verbal synthesis ( Li et al., 2026a ) . These findings motivate assessing training value separately from source quality. On-policy sampling and online preference learning connect data–policy compatibility to alignment outcomes ( Tajwar et al., 2024 ; Calandriello et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) . WPO reweights offline pairs using current-policy probabilities ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . InCo-DPO combines stronger-model prefixes with student continuations and selects pairs using reward-model scores ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . We adapt its continuation construction to speech as Bridge. Varying the expert-prefix ratio lets us compare target quality, likelihood, and generation outcomes.

sections.heading: 2.3 Likelihood Dynamics and Generation Quality
sections.text: Preference objectives modify likelihoods differently. SLiC-HF and RRHF calibrate or rank sequence likelihoods ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2023 ) , while IPO provides an alternative preference-learning formulation ( Gheshlaghi Azar et al., 2024 ) . ORPO and CPO combine preference learning with likelihood-based fitting, and SimPO uses length-normalized, reference-free rewards ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Meng et al., 2024 ) . APO addresses underspecified likelihood updates, and NCA distinguishes absolute likelihood optimization from relative comparisons ( D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . A larger preference margin can coexist with declining chosen likelihood ( Pal et al., 2024 ; Razin et al., 2025 ) , yet this decline need not imply worse generation ( Im et al., 2026 ) . Length effects and reward overoptimization further motivate separating training signals from outcome quality ( Park et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) . NISQA and UTMOS predict perceptual ratings; SpeechBERTScore compares generated and reference representations ( Mittag et al., 2021 ; Saeki et al., 2022 ; Saeki et al., 2024 ) . SpeechLMScore uses discrete-unit likelihood under a separately trained speech language model ( Maiti et al., 2023 ) . Our diagnostics track the student’s likelihood of fixed expert and initial-student probes across checkpoints, relating these changes to generation without equating them with perceptual improvement.

sections.heading: 3.1 Research Questions and Comparison Axes
sections.text: Here, β \beta scales the reference-relative preference score, following the standard DPO formulation (Appendix A.1 , Eq. 8 ). Three research questions examine expert supervision across objectives and routes: • RQ1: How sensitive are different preference objectives to the preference-score scale β \beta ? • RQ2: How do expert and initial-student likelihoods change, and how do these changes relate to generation outcomes? • RQ3: How do Direct–Bridge differences vary across objectives, expert sources, and students? DPO optimizes a relative preference margin, and WPO reweights that comparison ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . APO-zero and NCA act on chosen and rejected scores separately ( D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . We therefore measure both likelihood responses alongside generation outcomes.

sections.heading: Models and data.
sections.text: We use CosyVoice-1 (300M) and GPT-SoVITS v4 as students, with LibriTTS recordings and Qwen3-TTS (1.7B) generations as expert sources ( Du et al., 2024 ; Zen et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Expert speech is encoded into each student’s native representation. Training uses train-clean-100 , and ratio assessment uses dev-clean . Generation evaluation uses fixed 4–10-second subsets of LibriTTS test-clean and English SEED TTS Eval ( Anastassiou et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Training configurations.
sections.text: For RQ1–RQ2, we compare all four objectives at β ∈ { 0.01 , 0.1 } \beta\in\{0.01,0.1\} using CosyVoice with real-speech supervision. For RQ3, we fix β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 and compare both routes across students and expert sources. Direct trains for two epochs with full expert targets and fixed initial-student negatives. Bridge uses one epoch with partial-expert targets, followed by one epoch with full expert targets and regenerated intermediate-student negatives. First-phase ratios are r = 0.6 r=0.6 for CosyVoice–real, r = 0.8 r=0.8 for CosyVoice–Qwen, r = 0.4 r=0.4 for GPT-SoVITS–real, and r = 0.8 r=0.8 for GPT-SoVITS–Qwen.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We report utterance-level macro WER (%), speaker similarity (SIM), and NISQA predicted speech quality ( Mittag et al., 2021 ) . The ratio plot also reports character error rate (CER). Table 1 separately reports corpus-level WER for target characterization. The two aggregations are not directly interchangeable. Fixed-probe likelihood changes use full-expert and initial-student sequences, independently of phase-specific training pairs. Results are point estimates; we distinguish their magnitude and direction without claiming statistical significance. Unless accompanied by confidence intervals, results are point estimates and small differences are interpreted cautiously. All NLL measurements, conditional KL measurements, and paired speaker-bootstrap comparisons use the same shared pool of 1,000 utterance IDs across objectives, routes, and checkpoints. Bootstrap intervals quantify uncertainty in generation-metric differences. Conditional KL is measured relative to the original pretrained base on fixed teacher-forced contexts.

sections.heading: 5.1 Objective-Dependent Sensitivity to β \beta
sections.text: Table 2 shows that reducing β \beta from 0.1 0.1 to 0.01 0.01 substantially degrades DPO and WPO in this setting.. For DPO, LibriTTS WER rises from 4.59 % 4.59\% to 29.78 % 29.78\% , and SEED TTS Eval WER from 6.33 % 6.33\% to 63.02 % 63.02\% . WPO shows the same pattern, with WER increasing from 4.81 % 4.81\% to 25.57 % 25.57\% and from 6.58 % 6.58\% to 49.08 % 49.08\% , respectively. Both objectives also lose speaker similarity and predicted speech quality. APO-zero and NCA show smaller changes across the same two values. Their LibriTTS WER remains between 3.67 % 3.67\% and 3.77 % 3.77\% , compared with 3.87 % 3.87\% for the pretrained base. The tested β \beta reduction therefore has markedly different consequences across objectives . These results establish local sensitivity in one student–expert setting; two values do not establish a stability range or an optimal β \beta for any objective. A shared numerical β \beta is a comparison condition, not evidence that different losses induce matched update strengths. We use β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 in the remaining comparisons and examine how the contrasting generation outcomes relate to likelihood changes.

sections.heading: 5.2 Likelihood Responses and Their Limits
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , at β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 , DPO and WPO decrease mean token log-likelihood on expert probes by 0.348 0.348 and 0.295 0.295 , respectively, whereas APO-zero and NCA increase it by 0.083 0.083 and 0.033 0.033 . This difference extends beyond the mean: no evaluated expert probes gain likelihood under DPO or WPO, compared with 99.8 % 99.8\% under APO-zero and 96.0 % 96.0\% under NCA. All four objectives, however, decrease likelihood on 99.9 99.9 – 100 % 100\% of initial-student probes. Initial-student suppression therefore occurs both when WER improves over the base and when it deteriorates. Within this setting, expert-probe responses distinguish these outcomes more clearly than initial-student suppression. The expert-probe distinction persists at β = 0.01 \beta=0.01 : the positive-change rates are 0 % 0\% for DPO/WPO and 97.7 % / 97.6 % 97.7\%/97.6\% for APO-zero/NCA. Yet a large decrease on initial-student probes is not sufficient to identify poor generation. APO-zero decreases their mean log-likelihood by 9.243 9.243 , more than WPO’s 8.446 8.446 , while their LibriTTS WERs are 3.77 % 3.77\% and 25.57 % 25.57\% . Neither the prevalence nor the magnitude of initial-student suppression alone distinguishes these outcomes. The expert-probe responses are consistent with the objectives’ different structures. DPO/WPO optimize relative preference scores without requiring a likelihood increase for the chosen response, while APO-zero and NCA act on chosen and rejected scores separately. NCA additionally counterbalances chosen-score growth. This comparison characterizes the observed updates; it does not establish that the likelihood changes cause the generation differences. The following cross-setting comparisons test the limits of interpreting these diagnostics.

sections.heading: Real-speech supervision.
sections.text: Tables 3 and 4 show that Bridge reduces the LibriTTS WER deterioration of DPO/WPO for both students. For CosyVoice, DPO WER decreases from 4.59 % 4.59\% under Direct to 4.26 % 4.26\% under Bridge, and WPO from 4.81 % 4.81\% to 4.18 % 4.18\% . Both remain above the base WER of 3.87 % 3.87\% . For GPT-SoVITS, the corresponding changes are 18.12 % 18.12\% to 9.50 % 9.50\% and 13.03 % 13.03\% to 9.49 % 9.49\% , approaching the base value of 9.50 % 9.50\% . Figure 4 shows the corresponding DPO distributions. This mitigation accompanies smaller expert-probe likelihood losses for CosyVoice and a change from loss to gain for GPT-SoVITS DPO. Yet the latter’s expert-probe gain of 0.102 0.102 does not translate into better-than-base WER: Bridge matches the displayed LibriTTS baseline and reaches 4.87 % 4.87\% on SEED TTS Eval, above the base’s 4.27 % 4.27\% . Recovery from Direct’s deterioration should therefore be distinguished from improvement over the starting model. Benefits do not extend uniformly across evaluation sets: GPT-SoVITS WPO worsens on SEED TTS Eval, from 4.58 % 4.58\% to 5.49 % 5.49\% . sections.heading: Synthetic-expert supervision.
sections.text: With Qwen3-TTS supervision, CosyVoice Direct DPO/WPO improve WER over the base on both evaluation sets, despite decreasing expert-probe likelihood. DPO reduces LibriTTS WER from 3.87 % 3.87\% to 3.27 % 3.27\% and SEED TTS Eval WER from 4.27 % 4.27\% to 2.60 % 2.60\% , while expert-probe Δ ​ ℓ = − 0.318 \Delta\ell=-0.318 . Bridge reduces this likelihood loss to − 0.164 -0.164 , but increases WER to 4.27 % 4.27\% and 3.48 % 3.48\% , respectively. Thus, neither the sign of expert fitting relative to the base nor its improvement over Direct orders these generation outcomes. Together with GPT-SoVITS under real-speech supervision, these cases show why the likelihood–generation association observed in one setting cannot serve as a general route-selection criterion. GPT-SoVITS shows a different pattern with the same synthetic expert. Bridge lowers LibriTTS WER for DPO, WPO, and NCA, but slightly raises it for APO-zero. SEED TTS Eval changes are also mixed: WPO/NCA improve, whereas DPO/APO-zero worsen. These comparisons answer RQ3 by identifying setting-dependent mitigation and gains, rather than a consistently superior route.

sections.heading: 5.4 Checkpoint Analysis of Bridge Training
sections.text: We examine where the CosyVoice–Qwen Bridge route loses its Phase 1 gains. Figure 5 reports paired WER differences on the shared 1,000-utterance pool. For DPO and WPO, Phase 2 increases WER relative to Phase 1 by 1.04 percentage points (95% CI: [ 0.68 , 1.50 ] [0.68,1.50] ) and 1.01 points ( [ 0.68 , 1.39 ] [0.68,1.39] ), respectively, and also underperforms Direct training. Relative to the pretrained base, WPO’s WER increase has an interval excluding zero, whereas DPO’s interval includes zero. APO-zero and NCA show no clearly resolved phase difference and retain lower final WER than the base. The stage-specific likelihood measurements in Table 11 characterize the accompanying updates. During Phase 2, DPO/WPO substantially decrease rejected-response likelihood while producing little net change in mean chosen-target likelihood. Rejecting generations from the improved intermediate policy may discourage useful Phase 1 behavior without a corresponding increase in expert fitting. However, Phase 1 can improve WER despite declining chosen likelihood, and NCA remains stable despite little mean chosen-likelihood change. Neither rejected-response suppression nor weak expert fitting alone explains the deterioration. Table 5 provides a further counterexample through conditional KL measurements. Direct DPO/WPO have larger KL to the pretrained base than their final Bridge checkpoints on both fixed context sets, yet achieve lower WER. sections.heading: 5.5 Differences Across Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Generation metrics also favor different configurations. Under synthetic supervision, CosyVoice Direct WPO improves LibriTTS WER from the base’s 3.87 % 3.87\% to 3.22 % 3.22\% and NISQA from 4.484 4.484 to 4.543 4.543 , while SIM falls from 0.731 0.731 to 0.715 0.715 . For GPT-SoVITS with real-speech supervision, Direct APO-zero improves SEED TTS Eval WER from 4.27 % 4.27\% to 3.83 % 3.83\% and SIM from 0.401 0.401 to 0.411 0.411 , but lowers NISQA from 3.986 3.986 to 3.940 3.940 . Intelligibility gains therefore need not coincide with gains in speaker similarity or predicted speech quality. A single claim of “better speech” would conceal these trade-offs. Across RQ2–RQ3, fixed-probe diagnostics describe target fitting, while generation metrics establish observed benefits. Their relationship varies by student, expert source, route, and evaluation set; neither expert likelihood nor a single generation metric fully ranks the tested configurations.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Expert supervision for TTS requires more than selecting an appealing demonstration. Our study distinguishes the quality of expert speech, the student’s fitting of fixed targets, and the quality of its subsequent generations. Across the evaluated settings, these quantities do not provide interchangeable evidence of improvement. Preference objectives respond differently to the tested score scales, and staged Bridge supervision can mitigate degradation without surpassing the pretrained base. Most directly, increased expert likelihood can accompany worse intelligibility, while decreased likelihood can accompany better generation. The practical implication is to assess expert supervision through complementary generation metrics and explicit comparisons with the starting model. Fixed-probe likelihoods help describe what optimization changes; their value lies in interpreting those changes alongside generated speech, rather than certifying training success.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our study examines two student models and two expert sources on English utterances. The findings are scoped to these models, sources, and evaluation settings; broader language and duration coverage remains for future work. Generation results are point estimates from task-specific comparisons, so small differences warrant cautious interpretation. Our route comparison uses a fixed two-phase Bridge protocol; more stages and adaptive supervision schedules remain to be explored.

sections.heading: Appendix A Background of Preference Optimization Algorithms
sections.text: We summarize the four preference optimization objectives considered in this study: DPO, WPO, APO-zero, and NCA.

sections.heading: A.1 Common Notation
sections.text: Let ( x , 𝐲 + , 𝐲 − ) (x,\mathbf{y}^{+},\mathbf{y}^{-}) denote a preference triple, where x x is the conditioning input and 𝐲 + \mathbf{y}^{+} and 𝐲 − \mathbf{y}^{-} are the chosen and rejected speech-token sequences, respectively. Let π θ \pi_{\theta} be the trainable policy and π ref \pi_{\mathrm{ref}} a frozen reference policy. The sequence log-likelihood is log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ x ) = ∑ j = 1 | 𝐲 | log ⁡ π θ ​ ( y j ∣ x , 𝐲 < j ) . \log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}\mid x)=\sum_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{y}|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid x,\mathbf{y}_{<j}). (7) Following the standard reference-based formulation, define u θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 ) = β ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ x ) π ref ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ x ) , u_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y})=\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathbf{y}\mid x)}, (8) where β > 0 \beta>0 scales the reference-relative score. We write u + = u θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 + ) u^{+}=u_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y}^{+}) , u − = u θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 − ) u^{-}=u_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y}^{-}) , and σ ⁡ ( z ) = ( 1 + e − z ) − 1 \sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1} . Each training objective averages the corresponding per-pair loss over the preference dataset.

sections.heading: A.2 Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
sections.text: DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) derives a direct policy-learning objective from KL-regularized reward maximization and a Bradley–Terry preference model. Its per-pair loss is ℒ DPO = − log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( u + − u − ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\log\sigma(u^{+}-u^{-}). (9) This formulation allows preference learning without training a separate reward model or performing an explicit reinforcement-learning rollout during each update. Intuitively, DPO encourages the chosen response to improve relative to the rejected response, after accounting for their likelihoods under the reference policy. Its objective depends on the score difference rather than either score individually. Consequently, a larger preference margin can arise from increasing chosen likelihood, decreasing rejected likelihood, or decreasing both while suppressing the rejected response more strongly. DPO therefore does not explicitly require chosen likelihood to increase relative to the reference.

sections.heading: A.3 Weighted Preference Optimization (WPO)
sections.text: WPO ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) addresses the discrepancy between offline preference data and the current policy by assigning policy-dependent weights to preference pairs. Its DPO-based form is ℒ WPO = sg ⁡ [ a θ ] ​ ℒ DPO , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WPO}}=\operatorname{sg}[a_{\theta}]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}, (10) where a θ a_{\theta} is a nonnegative pair weight and sg \operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. A basic length-normalized weighting construction is q θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 ) = exp ⁡ [ 1 | 𝐲 | ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐲 ∣ x ) ] , a θ = q θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 + ) ​ q θ ​ ( x , 𝐲 − ) . \begin{split}q_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y})&=\exp\left[\frac{1}{|\mathbf{y}|}\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}\mid x)\right],\\ a_{\theta}&=q_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y}^{+})q_{\theta}(x,\mathbf{y}^{-}).\end{split} (11) The original method additionally introduces calibrated weights that account for variation in policy confidence. The intuition is to give greater influence to pairs that are more compatible with the current policy, approximating aspects of on-policy learning while retaining an offline dataset. Detaching the weights prevents the model from reducing the loss by directly manipulating the weighting factor. WPO changes the relative contribution of training pairs but retains DPO’s relative-margin objective.

sections.heading: A.4 Anchored Preference Optimization (APO-zero)
sections.text: APO ( D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ) introduces objectives that specify the intended directions of chosen and rejected likelihood changes. We consider its APO-zero variant: ℒ APO ​ - ​ zero = 1 − σ ⁡ ( u + ) + σ ⁡ ( u − ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{APO\text{-}zero}}=1-\sigma(u^{+})+\sigma(u^{-}). (12) The additive constant does not affect optimization. Unlike DPO, APO-zero acts on the two scores separately. It encourages chosen likelihood to increase relative to the reference and rejected likelihood to decrease. The zero anchor represents unchanged likelihood under the reference policy. Its sigmoid terms yield bounded losses and gradients that diminish as the individual scores move away from the anchor. This variant is motivated by settings in which the chosen responses are desirable examples for the policy to learn from.

sections.heading: A.5 Noise Contrastive Alignment (NCA)
sections.text: NCA ( Chen et al., 2024b ) formulates policy alignment through noise-contrastive estimation. Whereas DPO compares responses through a relative score difference, NCA learns individual reference-relative scores. Its binary-preference form is ℒ NCA = − log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( u + ) − 1 2 ​ log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( − u + ) − 1 2 ​ log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( − u − ) . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCA}}={}&-\log\sigma(u^{+})\\ &-\frac{1}{2}\log\sigma(-u^{+})-\frac{1}{2}\log\sigma(-u^{-}).\end{split} (13) The first term supports the chosen response, while the remaining terms account for the noise contribution of both responses. The chosen-response noise term counterbalances unrestricted score growth. Viewed as a loss over independent scores, NCA has a finite chosen-score optimum at u + = log ⁡ 2 u^{+}=\log 2 , while encouraging the rejected score to decrease. It therefore provides chosen support with a counterbalancing term, rather than optimizing only the pairwise margin.

sections.heading: A.6 Connection to Expert Supervision and Training Stability
sections.text: The objectives above differ in whether they optimize a relative margin, reweight that comparison, or act on individual reference-relative scores. These differences motivate examining chosen and rejected likelihood changes separately. However, objective-level incentives do not guarantee particular likelihood changes in a shared neural policy or improvements in generated-speech quality. Existing TTS studies likewise question whether higher-quality demonstrations necessarily provide better preference supervision. Tian et al. (2025) find that ranked model-generated pairs outperform ground-truth chosen responses, and report deterioration after an additional round of iterative optimization. Koel-TTS reports degeneration when ground-truth speech supplies chosen responses under its default DPO configuration ( Hussain et al., 2025 ) . These observations show that neither ground-truth targets nor additional optimization rounds guarantee better generation. Our study extends this evidence across objectives, students, expert sources, and Direct versus Bridge routes. We jointly examine demonstration quality after reconstruction, likelihood changes on fixed probes, and generated-speech quality. The comparisons identify settings in which expert fitting and intelligibility move in opposite directions, and distinguish mitigation of degradation from improvement over the pretrained base. Checkpoint analysis further localizes the loss of Bridge’s initial gains and examines whether conditional KL consistently ranks generation quality.

sections.heading: Model configurations.
sections.text: We initialize the students from the publicly released CosyVoice-1 300M 1 1 1 https://huggingface.co/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice-300M and GPT-SoVITS v4 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/lj1995/GPT-SoVITS checkpoints. Preference training performs full parameter fine-tuning of the autoregressive speech-token generation model: the LLM in CosyVoice and the GPT/Text2Semantic model in GPT-SoVITS. The remaining speech-processing and waveform-generation components are kept fixed. Synthetic expert speech is generated using Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base. 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base

sections.heading: Optimization settings.
sections.text: Both students use Adam with a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , batch size 2, zero weight decay, no gradient accumulation, and no warm-up. Gradients are clipped to a maximum norm of 5. Direct training runs for two epochs, while Bridge training uses one epoch per phase. We use β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 unless explicitly varied in the β \beta ablation. The objectives operate on summed sequence log-probabilities, including speech tokens, copied expert prefixes, and EOS, while excluding conditioning positions and padding. Parabolic policy-support weighting is applied across objectives and training routes, except when explicitly varied in the weighting ablation.

sections.heading: Training routes.
sections.text: All objectives and routes use the same retained training inputs within each student–expert setting. Direct pairs full expert targets with initial-student generations. Bridge first trains on constructed Bridge targets paired with initial-student generations, then trains on full expert targets paired with negatives regenerated by the corresponding intermediate student. Phase 2 starts from the Phase 1 model parameters with a newly initialized optimizer. The reference policy remains a frozen copy of the original pretrained student throughout both phases.

sections.heading: Appendix D Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We follow CosyVoice 3’s CV3-Eval evaluation tools for content consistency and speaker similarity 4 4 4 https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CV3-Eval . All metrics are averaged across evaluated utterances.

sections.heading: Word Error Rate (WER).
sections.text: We transcribe generated English speech using Whisper-large-v3 5 5 5 https://huggingface.co/openai/whisper-large-v3 and compare it with the intended text. WER is the number of word substitutions, deletions, and insertions divided by the reference word count. We report macro WER, the average of utterance-level error rates. Lower is better.

sections.heading: Speaker Similarity (SIM).
sections.text: We compute cosine similarity between speaker embeddings of generated and reference speech using ERes2Net 6 6 6 https://github.com/modelscope/3D-Speaker . The speaker reference for each input is fixed across configurations. Higher is better.

sections.heading: Speech Quality (NISQA).
sections.text: We use NISQA ( Mittag et al., 2021 ) , a non-intrusive speech-quality predictor, to estimate overall perceptual quality without a reference recording. Higher scores indicate better predicted quality.

NCA also produces little change in mean chosen NLL, with gains on 50.7 % 50.7\% of examples. APO-zero exhibits a more consistent increase in chosen likelihood: mean NLL decreases from 2.158 2.158 to 2.113 2.113 , with gains on 98.8 % 98.8\% of examples. These checkpoint comparisons locate the observed DPO/WPO WER deterioration in Phase 2, without establishing its cause. Because preference pairs and reference checkpoints differ across stages, the likelihood statistics characterize updates within each stage. They should not be interpreted as a fixed-trajectory comparison across checkpoints.

sections.text: We compute percentile 95% intervals from 10,000 paired speaker-bootstrap replicates. Each replicate samples speakers with replacement, retains their utterances with multiplicity, and recomputes macro-WER differences using identical resampled IDs across systems. Intervals capture evaluation-sample uncertainty, not training-seed variability. Figure 5 confirms that DPO/WPO lose their Phase 1 gains and underperform Direct training. Their Phase 2 WER increases relative to Phase 1 are 1.04 percentage points (95% CI: [ 0.68 , 1.50 ] [0.68,1.50] ) and 1.01 points ( [ 0.68 , 1.39 ] [0.68,1.39] ), respectively. APO-zero/NCA retain lower WER than the base, but their intervals establish neither a Phase 2 benefit nor equivalence between phases.

Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore Email: dcswangy@nus.edu.sg Abstract Preference optimization promises to improve text-to-speech (TTS) systems by learning which speech outputs are better. External expert speech seems a natural source of preferred responses, especially when student generations contain errors. Yet demonstration quality does not establish whether the student can benefit from that supervision, or whether better target fitting will produce better speech. We examine this gap across two TTS students using real and synthetic expert speech, comparing preference objectives and direct versus bridge supervision while tracking fixed-sequence likelihoods and generation metrics. With expert supervision held fixed, objectives differ markedly in their sensitivity to preference-score scaling and the resulting generation quality. Likelihood diagnostics characterize these responses, but cannot establish their benefit: expert likelihood can increase while intelligibility worsens, or decrease while it improves. Bridge supervision highlights a distinction between mitigating degradation and improving the student: it can recover performance lost under direct training without consistently surpassing the pretrained base. Route benefits vary across objectives, students, and expert sources; neither route consistently dominates. Together, these findings distinguish demonstration quality, target fitting, and generated-speech quality as complementary criteria for assessing expert supervision. 1 Introduction Preference optimization offers text-to-speech (TTS) systems a way to learn which speech outputs to prefer. Language-model-based TTS enables this approach through speech-token prediction ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Peng et al., 2024 ; Casanova et al., 2024 ; Du et al., 2024 ; Anastassiou et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from chosen–rejected pairs without a separately trained reward model ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , and has been applied to speech generation ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Its appeal, however, depends on where those preferred responses come from. Figure 1: Motivating questions for expert-guided preference optimization. Schematic panels H1–H3 correspond to RQ1–RQ3: objective sensitivity, likelihood responses, and supervision routes. One option is to rank student generations using recognition or speaker metrics ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) . Another is to pair student generations with external demonstrations from real recordings or an expert synthesizer. We call the latter expert-guided preference optimization . Demonstrations supply preferred targets without ranking a pool of student candidates and can provide examples absent from that pool. The attraction is straightforward: teach the student to favor an expert’s response over its own. Whether this produces a better speech generator is less straightforward. Existing evidence cautions against equating demonstration quality with training benefit. TTS studies report limited gains from ground-truth chosen responses compared with ranked model outputs ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) , with related observations in non-verbal vocalization synthesis ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Expert speech must also pass through the student’s speech-token representation, which can alter its quality. During optimization, a larger preference margin can coexist with declining chosen-response likelihood ( Pal et al., 2024 ) ; such a decline need not imply worse generation ( Im et al., 2026 ) . These observations leave an empirical question: how does fitting expert targets relate to generation quality under different objectives and supervision routes? We study CosyVoice and GPT-SoVITS as students, with real recordings and Qwen3-TTS generations as expert sources. We compare DPO, Weighted Preference Optimization (WPO), Anchored Preference Optimization’s zero variant (APO-zero), and Noise Contrastive Alignment (NCA) ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . RQ1 examines sensitivity to the score scale β \beta , and RQ2 relates likelihood changes to generation outcomes. RQ3 asks how supervision routes affect these outcomes across objectives, expert sources, and students. We compare Direct training on full expert targets with a staged Bridge route. A Bridge target combines an expert prefix with a student-generated continuation, adapting a construction explored in InCo-DPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) to speech. This route introduces Bridge targets before full expert supervision and refreshes rejected responses between phases. The comparison evaluates the complete protocol. Fixed expert and initial-student probes make likelihood changes comparable across checkpoints even when training pairs change. Our study yields three findings about expert supervision: • Reconstruction can erode an expert’s intelligibility advantage, so source quality alone does not characterize the supervision received by the student. • Training benefits depend on the objective and supervision route: objectives differ in sensitivity to β \beta , while bridge supervision can mitigate degradation without consistently surpassing the pretrained base. • Expert-probe likelihood can increase while intelligibility worsens, or decrease while it improves; target fitting alone therefore cannot establish generation benefit. 2 Related Work 2.1 Post-Training for Speech Generation Speech post-training draws on reinforcement learning from human feedback ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) and PPO/GRPO policy optimization ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) . Seed-TTS, IndexTTS 2.5, and GLM-TTS optimize rewards for recognition accuracy, speaker consistency, or expressiveness ( Anastassiou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . Other work studies GRPO-based TTS and ASR-guided updates ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Hussain et al., 2026 ) , differentiable rewards ( Gao et al., 2025a ; Gao et al., 2025b ) , and metric optimization for diffusion synthesis and duration prediction ( Li et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . At inference, MSpoofTTS uses spoof detectors for pruning and reranking; TED-TTS controls emotion and duration without fine-tuning ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . DPO uses preference pairs; KTO uses individual desirability labels ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ) . Speech preferences often rank candidates by recognition or speaker metrics ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . UNO and RIO study unpaired feedback and reverse-inference supervision ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Hu et al., 2024 ) ; FPO and TKTO study fine-grained and targeted token-level optimization ( Yao et al., 2026 ; Kotoge and Sasaki, 2026 ) . Align-SLM uses semantic feedback for speech continuation ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , while non-verbal synthesis requires preferences sensitive to lexical content and vocal events ( Li et al., 2026a ) . We compare how objectives use external expert demonstrations. 2.2 Preference Data and Policy Compatibility Discrete latent learning ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ) and neural audio codecs ( Zeghidour et al., 2022 ; Défossez et al., 2022 ) support token-based audio modeling and reconstruction. AudioLM combines semantic and acoustic tokens for structure and acoustic detail ( Borsos et al., 2023 ) ; we evaluate expert speech before and after reconstruction through the student’s representation. SpeechAlign pairs encoded recordings with synthesized responses and refreshes the latter ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . However, ground-truth chosen responses yield limited benefits in some TTS studies ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hussain et al., 2025 ) ; ground-truth and hybrid targets can also underperform synthetic pairs in non-verbal synthesis ( Li et al., 2026a ) . These findings motivate assessing training value separately from source quality. On-policy sampling and online preference learning connect data–policy compatibility to alignment outcomes ( Tajwar et al., 2024 ; Calandriello et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) . WPO reweights offline pairs using current-policy probabilities ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) . InCo-DPO combines stronger-model prefixes with student continuations and selects pairs using reward-model scores ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . We adapt its continuation construction to speech as Bridge. Varying the expert-prefix ratio lets us compare target quality, likelihood, and generation outcomes. 2.3 Likelihood Dynamics and Generation Quality Preference objectives modify likelihoods differently. SLiC-HF and RRHF calibrate or rank sequence likelihoods ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2023 ) , while IPO provides an alternative preference-learning formulation ( Gheshlaghi Azar et al., 2024 ) . ORPO and CPO combine preference learning with likelihood-based fitting, and SimPO uses length-normalized, reference-free rewards ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Meng et al., 2024 ) . APO addresses underspecified likelihood updates, and NCA distinguishes absolute likelihood optimization from relative comparisons ( D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . A larger preference margin can coexist with declining chosen likelihood ( Pal et al., 2024 ; Razin et al., 2025 ) , yet this decline need not imply worse generation ( Im et al., 2026 ) . Length effects and reward overoptimization further motivate separating training signals from outcome quality ( Park et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) . NISQA and UTMOS predict perceptual ratings; SpeechBERTScore compares generated and reference representations ( Mittag et al., 2021 ; Saeki et al., 2022 ; Saeki et al., 2024 ) . SpeechLMScore uses discrete-unit likelihood under a separately trained speech language model ( Maiti et al., 2023 ) . Our diagnostics track the student’s likelihood of fixed expert and initial-student probes across checkpoints, relating these changes to generation without equating them with perceptual improvement. 3 Study Design 3.1 Research Questions and Comparison Axes Here, β \beta scales the reference-relative preference score, following the standard DPO formulation (Appendix A.1 , Eq. 8 ). Three research questions examine expert supervision across objectives and routes: • RQ1: How sensitive are different preference objectives to the preference-score scale β \beta ? • RQ2: How do expert and initial-student likelihoods change, and how do these changes relate to generation outcomes? • RQ3: How do Direct–Bridge differences vary across objectives, expert sources, and students? DPO optimizes a relative preference margin, and WPO reweights that comparison ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . APO-zero and NCA act on chosen and rejected scores separately ( D’Oosterlinck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) . We therefore measure both likelihood responses alongside generation outcomes. 3.2 Characterizing Expert Supervision Expert speech enters training through the student’s speech-token representation. Their relationship varies by student, expert source, route, and evaluation set; neither expert likelihood nor a single generation metric fully ranks the tested configurations. 6 Conclusion Expert supervision for TTS requires more than selecting an appealing demonstration. Our study distinguishes the quality of expert speech, the student’s fitting of fixed targets, and the quality of its subsequent generations. Across the evaluated settings, these quantities do not provide interchangeable evidence of improvement. Preference objectives respond differently to the tested score scales, and staged Bridge supervision can mitigate degradation without surpassing the pretrained base. Most directly, increased expert likelihood can accompany worse intelligibility, while decreased likelihood can accompany better generation. The practical implication is to assess expert supervision through complementary generation metrics and explicit comparisons with the starting model. Fixed-probe likelihoods help describe what optimization changes; their value lies in interpreting those changes alongside generated speech, rather than certifying training success. Limitations Our study examines two student models and two expert sources on English utterances. The findings are scoped to these models, sources, and evaluation settings; broader language and duration coverage remains for future work. Generation results are point estimates from task-specific comparisons, so small differences warrant cautious interpretation. Our route comparison uses a fixed two-phase Bridge protocol; more stages and adaptive supervision schedules remain to be explored. References Anastassiou et al. (2024) P. Anastassiou, J. Chen, J.
